articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License FF-1 for Iraq Development Bank
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran-related General License FF-1, which amends and supersedes the previous General License FF. This updated license authorizes the wind-down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, also known as Iraq Development Bank, and certain entities majority-owned by it.

The amended general license, effective October 29, 2026, sets a deadline of December 1, 2026, for the completion of these wind-down transactions. A key change in GL FF-1 is the requirement that any payments to blocked persons must now be made into blocked accounts.
This action is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to manage sanctions against Iran, while providing specific authorizations for certain financial activities.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions North Korean IT Worker Schemes and Rwandan Entities Supporting M23 in DRC
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has sanctioned ten individuals and one entity for their involvement in North Korean government-run IT worker schemes. These schemes defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for the DPRK's unlawful weapons programs.

The sanctioned individuals and entity are accused of using fraudulent documents, stolen identities, and fabricated personas to secure employment with legitimate companies, including those in the United States. OFAC highlighted that these networks leverage cryptocurrency transactions, money laundering techniques, and emerging technologies like artificial intelligence to generate and transfer funds.

In a separate action on the same day, OFAC also designated the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution. These designations were made for facilitating Rwanda's support for the March 23 Movement (M23) and its political wing in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to resolve potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of Russia sanctions.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer. OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed by Extreme Networks, Inc. and were egregious.
The settlement amount for these violations is $1,529,685.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Frequently Asked Questions on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update aims to provide clearer guidance to U.S. persons and financial institutions on their compliance obligations under OFAC regulations.

The amendments likely address common questions and scenarios encountered when dealing with blocked property or rejected transactions, ensuring that reporting requirements are met accurately and efficiently. These FAQs serve as a crucial resource for navigating the complexities of sanctions compliance.
The issuance of amended FAQs reflects OFAC's commitment to transparency and assisting the public in understanding and adhering to U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, further expanding sanctions against entities and individuals connected to the Iranian regime. This action is part of an ongoing campaign to exert economic pressure on Iran.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. This indicates a recalibration of sanctions policy concerning these countries.

Additionally, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions, providing updated guidance and authorizations for certain transactions under these sanctions programs.

articles.headline: PAIPA Designations Imposed with Associated General Licenses Issued
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations target individuals and entities involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property rights.

Alongside these designations, OFAC has issued associated General Licenses. These licenses are intended to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited by the new PAIPA sanctions, aiming to minimize unintended consequences while upholding the integrity of the sanctions program.
The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding American innovation and intellectual property from theft and illicit exploitation globally.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This action reflects ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions policy concerning Venezuela.

The amendment to the general license likely modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Venezuela, potentially impacting specific sectors or types of engagements. The accompanying FAQ provides clarification on the scope and application of these changes.
These updates are part of the U.S. government's dynamic approach to Venezuela sanctions, which has seen both easing and tightening of restrictions in response to political and economic developments.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, further targeting entities and individuals associated with the Iranian regime. These actions are part of the broader 'Operation Economic Outcast' campaign aimed at disrupting Iran's financial networks.

In a separate action, OFAC also imposed a new designation related to Cuba. This designation comes amidst a significant expansion and restructuring of U.S.-Cuba sanctions in recent months, including the introduction of new Cuba Sanctions Regulations.

Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions for both the Iran and Cuba sanctions programs, providing updated guidance and authorizations for certain transactions.

articles.headline: Venezuela-Related Designation Removed by OFAC
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action indicates a specific individual or entity has been delisted from OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List under the Venezuela sanctions program.

Designation removals can occur for various reasons, including a change in circumstances, successful appeals, or diplomatic considerations. This particular removal suggests a targeted adjustment within the broader Venezuela sanctions framework.

While this is a specific removal, the overall U.S. sanctions regime against Venezuela remains in effect, targeting the Venezuelan government, state-owned enterprises, and individuals involved in corruption or undermining democracy.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under its Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism sanctions programs. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing activities globally.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial networks and operations of criminal organizations and terrorist groups, preventing them from accessing the U.S. financial system and international markets.
The U.S. government continues to utilize its sanctions authorities to combat transnational criminal organizations and terrorist threats, underscoring its commitment to global security and stability.

articles.headline: EU Imposes 22nd Sanctions Package on Russia, Targeting Military-Industrial Complex
body: The Council of the European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia on October 12, 2026, marking the most significant round of listings since 2022. This package imposes sanctions on an additional 1,569 individuals and entities, bringing the total number of designations to 4,600.

The new measures primarily target Russia's military-industrial complex, including 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals. More than half of these listings are connected to ballistic missile production, and they extend to suppliers of dual-use technologies and components across various sectors, including automotive manufacturing and research.

These designations require assets belonging to listed persons to be frozen and prohibit making funds or economic resources available to them. The EU's strategy increasingly relies on targeted designations to disrupt Russia's military supply chains and address sanctions circumvention.

articles.headline: Iran and US Remain Far From Deal Despite Intensified Diplomatic Efforts
body: A senior Iranian official has stated that Iran and the United States remain far from a deal to end the ongoing conflict, despite intensified diplomatic efforts following the US midterm elections.

Overnight, the US reportedly carried out 'defensive' strikes on Iran's Qeshm island, targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets. US officials described these strikes as limited and not indicative of a resumption of major combat operations.

Qatar has stepped up its mediation efforts, with mediators traveling to Tehran for talks on a draft US-Iran deal. However, the Iranian official emphasized that Tehran's conditions must be met for the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened.

Experts suggest that deeper reforms are necessary to address the root causes of Lebanon's persistent electricity problems. The current situation is having a significant impact on daily life and public services.
The energy crisis is one of many economic and political challenges facing Lebanon, which has been struggling with instability and a lack of effective governance.

articles.headline: Al Jazeera Celebrates 30 Years of Transforming News, Launches New Ecosystem
body: Al Jazeera celebrated its 30th anniversary on November 1, 2026, marking three decades of what it describes as 'transforming news in Middle East and beyond.' The Qatari media network announced the launch of a new 'ecosystem' of channels during a celebration in Doha.

The network, which began broadcasting in Arabic on November 1, 1996, with an initial grant from the Qatari state, quickly gained popularity for its independent editorial approach in a region dominated by state-controlled media.
Al Jazeera has been recognized for its extensive coverage of major global events, including the invasion of Iraq, the Syrian civil war, the Arab Spring revolutions, and the conflict in Gaza.

articles.headline: OCC Challenges California Climate Disclosure Laws, Citing Federal Preemption
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has challenged California's new climate disclosure statutes, urging the California Air Resources Board (CARB) to exempt national banks and federal savings associations.
Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould argued in an October 29, 2026, letter that federal preemption and the OCC's exclusive visitorial authority over national banks should apply.

The OCC also raised concerns about disproportionate compliance burdens, particularly for community banks, and emphasized the importance of tailoring regulatory requirements to an institution's size and risk profile.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions Against Major Banks for BSA Violations
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced significant enforcement actions in October 2026, including a Cease and Desist Order and a Civil Money Penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah.

The actions against American Express National Bank were for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and violations related to customer due diligence and customer identification programs. The assessed civil money penalty is $350 million.

Additionally, the OCC imposed a Civil Money Penalty of $750 million against Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina, for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information.

Similarly, Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at the La Mirada, California Operations Center of U.S. Bank National Association, Cincinnati, Ohio, was prohibited for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
